claim: Human and other animal cells deploy three closely related dioxygenases (PHD 1, 2 and 3) to signal oxygen levels by catalysing oxygen regulated prolyl hydroxylation of the transcription factor HIF.
source: Human and other animal cells deploy three closely related dioxygenases (PHD 1, 2 and 3) to signal oxygen levels by catalysing oxygen regulated prolyl hydroxylation of the transcription factor HIF.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the HIF prolyl hydroxylase system, supported by the review citations provided in the introduction.

claim: Prolyl hydroxylation promotes the association of HIF-α with the von-Hippel-Lindau ubiquitin E3 ligase (pVHL) and subsequent degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.
source: Prolyl hydroxylation promotes the association of HIF-α with the von-Hippel-Lindau ubiquitin E3 ligase (pVHL) and subsequent degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HIF regulatory pathway, supported by review citations.

claim: PHD-catalysed hydroxylation is highly sensitive to the availability of oxygen and provides an 'oxygen-sensing' mechanism.
source: PHD-catalysed hydroxylation is highly sensitive to the availability of oxygen and provides an 'oxygen-sensing' mechanism that, via HIF, regulates a wide range of cellular and systemic responses to oxygen, including those (e.g. blood haematocrit) that operate precisely around the 'set-point' of physiological oxygen availability (for reviews, see Schofield and Ratcliffe, 2004; Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008; Myllyharju, 2013; Semenza, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on the oxygen sensing mechanism.

claim: More than 20 potential non-HIF substrates of PHDs have been reported to date.
source: More than 20 potential non-HIF substrates have been reported to date (German et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2014; Xie et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2016; Köditz et al., 2007; Moser et al., 2015; Moser et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2015; Heir et al., 2016; Segura et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2014; Cummins et al., 2006; Rodriguez et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2015; Huo et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2011; Mikhaylova et al., 2008; Di Conza et al., 2017; Anderson et al., 2011; Xie et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2015; Ullah et al., 2017; Rodriguez et al., 2018; Takahashi et al., 2011) (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies and summarized in Table 1.

claim: No PHD-catalysed prolyl hydroxylation was detected on any reported non-HIF protein or peptide using conditions supporting robust HIF-α hydroxylation.
source: Unexpectedly, we did not detect prolyl-hydroxylase activity on any reported non-HIF protein or peptide, using conditions supporting robust HIF-α hydroxylation.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by extensive experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each PHD isoform catalysed near complete hydroxylation of the positive control HIF-1α peptide.
source: Each PHD isoform catalysed near complete hydroxylation of the positive control HIF-1α peptide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide hydroxylation assays.

claim: No PHD isoform catalysed detectable hydroxylation of any non-HIF peptide tested.
source: By contrast, no PHD isoform catalysed detectable hydroxylation of any other peptide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide hydroxylation assays analyzed by MS.

claim: A total of 44 non-HIF peptides representing putative sites of prolyl hydroxylation within 23 reported protein substrates were tested.
source: A total of 44 non-HIF peptides representing putative sites of prolyl hydroxylation within 23 reported protein substrates were tested in this way.
evidence: This describes the scope of the experimental work conducted.

claim: Enzyme independent oxidations were observed on certain peptides but did not increase in reactions containing PHD enzymes compared to control reactions without enzyme.
source: Inspection of the MS spectra revealed apparent oxidation (i.e. a +16 Da mass shift relative to the unmodified substrate) on certain peptides, for example ACTB/310–334 (Figure 1). However, in no case was an increase in the apparent oxidation detectable in reactions containing PHD enzymes, when compared with control reactions without enzyme.
evidence: This is supported by MS data showing oxidations that are not enzyme-dependent.

claim: Robust PHD-dependent hydroxylation was detected on HIF-1α at P402 and P564, HIF-2α at P405 and P531, and HIF-3α at P492 with PHD1 and PHD2.
source: These experiments confirmed robust prolyl hydroxylation at P402 and P564 in HIF-1α, P405 and P531 in HIF-2α and P492 in HIF-3α, with both PHD1 and PHD2 and robust hydroxylation of HIF-1α P564, HIF-2α P531 and HIF-3α P492, but not at the other two sites for PHD3, consistent with the known site specificity of PHD3 (Figure 2 and supplements).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from IVTT hydroxylation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: PHD3 had little activity on HIF-1α P402, consistent with known HIF substrate specificity.
source: note that PHD1 and PHD2 catalysed hydroxylations at both P402 and P564, whereas PHD3 had little activity on P402, consistent with known HIF substrate specificity (Hirsilä et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and cited literature on PHD substrate specificity.

claim: Prolyl hydroxylation was not assigned on any of the reported non-HIF substrate sites by MS software search, even though the non-oxidised target peptide was always identified.
source: By contrast, prolyl hydroxylation was not assigned on any of the reported non-HIF substrate sites by the software search, even though the non-oxidised target peptide was always identified.
evidence: This is supported by MS data analysis of IVTT-derived substrates.

claim: Putative hydroxylations on non-HIF substrates were most frequently assigned to methionine residues, but also included aspartate and di-hydroxylation of tryptophan.
source: A number of peptides spanning the reported site of prolyl hydroxylation bore putative hydroxylations (i.e. +16 Da mass increments) that could be assigned to residues other than proline. These were most frequently on methionine, but also included aspartate and di-hydroxylation of tryptophan; in three substrates the putative oxidation event could not be localised to a specific residue.
evidence: This is supported by MS data analysis showing oxidations on non-proline residues.

claim: Neither the assigned oxidations nor putative oxidised species were significantly increased by reaction with the relevant PHD.
source: Neither the assigned oxidations, nor these putative oxidised species were significantly increased by reaction with the relevant PHD.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MS data comparing control and PHD-reacted samples.

claim: No PHD-dependent hydroxylation was detected on any of the polypeptides using radiochemical assays for hydroxyproline.
source: Despite the presence of only two target prolyl residues in HIF-1α, robust PHD-dependent hydroxylation was detected. However, no PHD-dependent hydroxylation was detected on any of the other polypeptides.
evidence: This is supported by radiochemical assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Related peptide sets displayed broadly comparable ion counts between prolyl and hydroxyprolyl forms.
source: Accordingly, peptide intensities were quantified by peak area integration of extracted ion chromatograms and expressed as relative ratios. Related peptide sets displayed broadly comparable ion counts, as summarised in Table 2—source data 1.
evidence: This is supported by MS analysis of synthetic peptide standards.

claim: A reproducible shift in chromatographic retention between related pairs of prolyl and hydroxyprolyl peptides was observed, ranging from −0.14 to −4.72 min.
source: A reproducible shift in chromatographic retention between related pairs of prolyl and hydroxyprolyl peptides was observed. This shift was variable across peptide pairs, ranging from −0.14 to −4.72 min for a given hydroxyprolyl modification resolved on a 60 min linear gradient (Table 2—source data 1.).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS analysis of synthetic peptide standards.

claim: Despite robust detection of diagnostic fragment ions derived from hydroxyprolyl peptide standards, no such ions were observed in the IVTT material either before or after reaction with the relevant PHD enzyme.
source: Despite robust detection of diagnostic fragment ions derived from hydroxyprolyl peptide standards, no such ions were observed in the IVTT material either before or after reaction with the relevant PHD enzyme.
evidence: This is supported by parallel reaction monitoring MS data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Among 12.8 million assigned spectra from cellular proteome analyses, only 67 spectra were assigned as potential prolyl hydroxylations on non-HIF substrates, all of which were of low confidence.
source: Among 12.8 million assigned spectra, we observed a total of 18,192 that corresponded to the trypsinolysis-derived peptides containing the proposed site(s) of prolyl hydroxylation in 17 of the non-HIF PHD substrates; in the remaining six substrates the target peptide was not identified. A total of 5038 putative singly oxidised peptides were assigned among 13 of these 17 identified sequences. Only 67 of these spectra were assigned as potential prolyl hydroxylations. However, inspection of the data revealed that all the computationally assigned putative prolyl oxidations were either at low fragment ion intensity and/or of low confidence with respect to the localisation of the oxidised residue.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of deposited cellular proteome MS data.

claim: There are no high confidence proline oxidation assignments meeting both AScore and Ion Intensity thresholds of the reported substrates in cellular proteome data.
source: There are no high confidence proline oxidation assignments (i.e., meeting both AScore and Ion Intensity thresholds) of the reported substrates, suggesting a high degree of uncertainty from the software.
evidence: This is stated in Table 3 caption and supported by the analysis of cellular proteome data.

claim: A high prevalence of oxidation, some of which was computer assigned as hydroxyproline, was observed on several unmodified synthetic peptide standards.
source: These analyses revealed a high prevalence of oxidation, some of which was computer assigned as hydroxyproline, on several of the peptides, including ACTB residues 316–326, AKT1 residues 308–328, and MAPK6 residues 20–45 (Table 3—source data 1.).
evidence: This is supported by MS analysis of synthetic peptide standards showing artefactual oxidations.

claim: Most (possibly all) HIF-α peptides are predicted to form an α-helix to the N-terminal side of the target prolyl residue.
source: This revealed that despite considerable variation in primary sequence, most (possibly all) HIF-α peptides are predicted to form an α-helix to the N-terminal side of the target prolyl residue, as was observed in PHD2-HIF-α complex structures.
evidence: This is supported by secondary structure prediction analysis shown in Table 1—source data 2.

claim: The α-helical feature N-terminal to the target proline was seen in few of the reported non-HIF substrates, where no clear pattern was evident.
source: In contrast, this feature was seen in few of the reported non-HIF substrates, where no clear pattern was evident.
evidence: This is supported by secondary structure prediction analysis shown in Table 1—source data 2.

claim: The existence of multiple non-HIF substrates would predict that many non-HIF dependent biological systems would be regulated by oxygen.
source: If this were the case, it would be predicted: (i) that many non-HIF dependent biological systems would be regulated by oxygen
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of multiple non-HIF substrates.

claim: The existence of multiple non-HIF substrates would predict that PHD substrate competition might modulate the responses to hypoxia mediated by HIF.
source: (ii) that PHD substrate competition might modulate the responses to hypoxia mediated by HIF
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of multiple non-HIF substrates.

claim: The existence of multiple non-HIF substrates would predict that inhibitors of the PHDs would have multiple consequences unrelated to HIF.
source: (iii) that inhibitors of the PHDs, including those in clinical trials (for review see Maxwell and Eckardt, 2016; Gupta and Wish, 2017), would have multiple consequences unrelated to HIF.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of multiple non-HIF substrates, with citations to reviews on PHD inhibitors.

claim: The findings using recombinant enzymes provide no support for the wide range of non-HIF PHD substrates that have been reported.
source: However, our findings using recombinant enzymes provide no support for the wide range of non-HIF PHD substrates that have been reported.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the experimental data presented.

claim: It is possible that PHD-catalysed prolyl hydroxylation might occur under conditions other than those examined in this study.
source: We cannot exclude PHD-catalysed prolyl hydroxylation occurring under conditions other than those we have examined.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledging the limitations of the study.

claim: It is possible that some or all reported non-HIF substrates might require one or more adaptor molecules to promote hydroxylation.
source: It is also possible that PHD-catalysed hydroxylation might take place in cells but not in our assays. For instance, some or all reported non-HIF substrates might require one or more adaptor molecules, which are unnecessary for HIF substrates, to promote hydroxylation.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the negative results.

claim: FIH-catalysed asparaginyl hydroxylation of both HIF-α and non-HIF substrates was readily observed using the assays described in this work.
source: Consistent with this, FIH-catalysed asparaginyl hydroxylation of both HIF-α and non-HIF substrates was readily observed using the assays described in our current work (data not shown).
evidence: This is mentioned as unpublished data supporting the validity of the assay methods.

claim: FIH has been shown to catalyse hydroxylations at asparaginyl (and other) residues on a wide range of ankyrin repeat domain containing proteins, in addition to HIF-α.
source: This contrasts with the HIF asparaginyl hydroxylase, FIH (factor inhibiting HIF), which has been shown to catalyse hydroxylations at asparaginyl (and other) residues on a wide range of ankyrin repeat domain containing proteins, in addition to HIF-α (Chowdhury et al., 2016; Elkins et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on FIH substrate specificity.

claim: X-ray and NMR structural analyses reveal that HIF-α peptide bound to PHD makes multiple contacts with the enzyme.
source: X-ray and NMR structural analyses of HIF-α peptide in complex with the PHD catalytic domain reveal that the bound peptide makes multiple contacts with the enzyme (Chowdhury et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: There are substantial conformational changes in the PHD structures on binding HIF-α substrates, including a loop which moves to tightly enclose the catalytic site.
source: There are also substantial conformational changes in the PHD structures on binding HIF-α substrates, including a loop which moves to tightly enclose the catalytic site and C-terminal region of the enzyme (Chowdhury et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: FIH has a much more accessible catalytic site and does not demonstrate a major conformational change upon substrate binding, according to crystallographic studies.
source: These observations contrast with FIH, which crystallographic studies imply has a much more accessible catalytic site and does not itself demonstrate a major conformational change upon substrate binding (Elkins et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to crystallographic studies of FIH.

claim: The characteristics of PHDs likely contribute to their specificity for HIF-α substrates.
source: These characteristics of PHDs likely contribute to their specificity for HIF-α substrates, but make it difficult predict other substrates from the primary sequence.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural characteristics of PHDs.

claim: PHDs might have the capacity to generate major conformational changes in folded substrates, as described for the PHD homologue in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: Although such an α-helix may therefore contribute to selectivity for HIF-α and/or guide future attempts to identify non-HIF substrates of the PHDs, a caveat is that the PHDs might have the capacity to generate major conformational changes in folded substrates, such as have been described for the PHD homologue in Pseudomonas aeruginosa complexed with its EF-Tu (Elongation Factor Thermal unstable) substrate (Scotti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to a bacterial PHD homologue, supported by citation.
